title: Controlling Dark Squares | Sicilian, Accelerated Dragon | Top Theory Speedrun | GM Naroditsky

moves.spoken: My recommendation is the Accelerated Dragon. White surprises with c4 — think of it as an English where White plays c4, we play c5, and White plays e4. Its drawback jumps out: White has created a massive hole on d4 — a square no pawn can ever defend, since the c- and e-pawns have advanced past it.

This gives our knight a potential outpost on d4 — but a hole existing doesn't mean occupy it at once. We start with the knight to c6, not to play the knight to d4 next: it's too early, with nothing else developed.
The knight to f3 would just knock a d4-knight off. It's the long-term weakness that costs White later. We also get a massive diagonal for our dark-squared bishop.
We play g6 — though in a classical game I'd prefer e6 or the knight to f6, since g6 allows White to transition to main lines.
The drawback of g6: it allows d4 — after d4, c takes d4, knight takes d4, we transpose to the Maroczy Bind Accelerated Dragon. Since we're emphasizing openings, I wouldn't mind. White plays d3.
Objectively, to punish c4 you don't allow that transposition — you pressure e4 and stop White getting a good d4.
Our opponent played d3, solidifying the d4 hole.
After the bishop to g7, we're flat-out better: great pieces, dominating the dark squares, and White's light bishop is now a big pawn.

The knight to c3. We develop normally. It's self-evidently good to trade our light bishop for White's f3-knight — visualize it gone: our control of d4 increases, and we can contemplate the knight to d4, though White can still trade it with the dark bishop or the c3-knight, both awkward.
The best way to threaten that trade is d6 — a normal developing move I like more than the knight to f6, which I'll delay. White plays the bishop to e3.
We develop the bishop to g4, continuing to clamp d4, trading a piece that controls it — classic positional chess.
The bishop to e2. Do we take on f3 or wait? It doesn't matter — both are good.
I'll eliminate the knight while we can, capturing on f3 — the drawback of waiting is that the knight could move away.
White recaptures, capturing on f3.

Trading light bishops is okay, but not as glamorous as removing White's knight. And there's no hurry for the knight to d4 — after the knight to d4, the bishop takes d4, we recapture and get uncontested dark squares, but let's practice restraint.

The knight to d4 is solid, but instead we find a developing square for the g8-knight that doesn't obstruct our own control of d4 — the drawback of the knight to f6, which might then have to drop to d7. Play the Sicilian enough and you know the Botvinnik setup.

The Botvinnik setup: fianchetto the dark bishop, then carve a square for the g8-knight with e6, keeping the bishop unobstructed. The e6 pawn is an asset, controlling d5 and f5 — a toothy central construction.
Our pawns are like teeth controlling key squares. e5 would be bad — it returns the favor, creating a d5 hole and blocking the bishop.

So the knight to e7 — notice how harmoniously our pieces sit. In the Sicilian you usually avoid e6 and g6 together, but that's when the centre is OPEN and it creates dark-square holes; here the centre is closed, so those holes are inaccessible.
White can play the knight to b5 — a paper tiger, chase it with a6. And we don't worry about weakening the d6 pawn, well protected by the queen. The bishop to g5.
The d6 pawn is essentially unattackable.

I'm not afraid of White taking on e7 — that's what we want: White gives away the dark bishop for our e7-knight, the inferior piece, leaving the other knight to reach d4. So we prod White with h6. I don't love castling kingside first because of the queen to d2, threatening to trade the dark bishops — a serious positional threat we don't want.
So h6 does two things: it provokes the trade on e7, and if White retreats to h4 instead, we can castle kingside without fearing the bishop-h6 battery.
We recapture with the queen, keeping the knight's access to d4 — and we don't fear the king-queen alignment, since the centre is closed.
The queen to a4 pins the knight. Our next move is obvious.
We castle, exiting the opening — Black is much better, maybe minus 1.5 or 2. Notice the dark-square control; White can't move, stuck with a bad bishop. Now we convert.

How to convert abstract positional advantages? The knight to d4 is a move, not a plan. There's a stock plan here: a queenside pawn storm opening files — when your pieces are better placed, opening flanks favors you.

The break is b5, prepared with a6 — an unassuming move. And b5 is already available: after b5, c takes b5, a takes b5, queen takes b5, the knight jumps to d4, ruining the kingside structure or even reaching c2. The moment a rook appeared on e1, I am eyeing the knight jumping to c2. This a6-b5 plan is universal in anti-Sicilians.

We don't rush the knight to d4, keeping it for the right moment. White plays h3, doing nothing about b5. I like the knight to d4 first: then the bishop has only d1, since after the bishop to g4 we chase with h5; then b5 virtually traps the queen — c2 and b3 are covered by the knight, and if the queen goes to a3, b4 forks. b5 immediately is slightly inaccurate, letting the queen drop to d1.

After b5, the queen to d1, the knight to d4, you no longer threaten the knight-takes-f3 check, so the effect is diminished. After the knight to d4, a strong player plays the queen to d1, White's only non-losing move — hard to find, since moving the bishop back seems natural. It's worth starting with the knight to d4, more flexible, testing White — being practical, not tricky.
The rook to e3 is possible, but we still play b5, and after it, h5 with the bishop-h6 idea chases the rook. The bishop to d1.
Boom — we strike with b5, and White is borderline lost.
White takes on b5.
We recapture on b5, and the queen is literally trapped. That's how quickly typical plans work when you know them. White must give the queen for a rook — the queen takes a8.
That's the best move technically, and we keep all our advantages, so it's completely lost. The queen to a5 is the only try, but we can nearly trap it with b4 and the knight to c6.
The queen takes a8.
The rook recaptures on a8.
a3 — fine with us, we continue the plan: expand on the queenside, open files.

b4 is begging to be played, especially since White's rooks are disconnected so a takes b4 is impossible. The knight to e2. Two plans now: simplify, or my preferred, keep the tension — don't trade our better rook needlessly.
Our queen is stuck in no man's land — it could go to b7 to x-ray b2, but I'm looking at White's king: the queen to g5, threatening the knight-f3 check, with a second idea of infiltrating to d2.
The rook to a2 doesn't defend the knight-f3 threat.
The knight to f3 with check.
The second idea was the queen to d2.
If White had gone the knight-e2 to g3, we'd infiltrate to d2 with the queen, forking the rook and b2, winning immediately.
But this ends it right away — notice how quickly we won, boom boom.
Whereas simplifying with the take on a3 would have dragged it out.
...the king to f1...
The knight takes the rook.
We take the rook — the king recaptures. Up a full queen, simplification is now almost always justified, though not necessary.
I threw in b takes a3 just to clarify the queenside.
We grab another free pawn, capturing on g2 — not just free, it wrecks White's kingside. Take free stuff when it presents itself.
Don't fear the a-pawn — it's going nowhere.
The a8-rook stops it; even at a7 we'd pick it off. So keep taking — the queen takes h3.
a5, and we take another pawn on d3.
The queen takes d3 — funnily, it also prevents a6.
Always follow through with a question when you fear something — figure out exactly why, and whether you should. The bishop to c2.
The queen drops back to c4, attacking the rook, pressuring the bishop, keeping contact with the knight.
...the rook to a4...
The queen takes the bishop — thank you. Hopefully White resigns.
The queen takes a4.
Let's go over it. c4 on move two isn't such a bad move if White follows up accurately.
After the knight to c6, the knight to f3...
...a comment on g6 technically not being best...
...because it lets White transition back into open-Sicilian channels.

...c takes d4, the knight recaptures — the Maroczy Bind, where theory says White is better, defined by the c4 pawn versus the traditional knight to c3. This is usually reached via the open move order. In a classical game I'd play e6 — after d4 you get a bad Maroczy, with the knight to f6 in and White's centre under pressure.
